rows.text: ATP synthase. The enzyme that makes ATP, built into the inner membrane of the mitochondrion. Protons falling across the membrane spin its rotor about a hundred times a second, and each turn assembles ATP from ADP and phosphate.

Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. The sodium-potassium pump, in the membrane of every animal cell. It spends one ATP to push three sodium ions out and pull two potassium ions in, which is what keeps a cell electrically charged and costs about a fifth of the energy you use at rest.

Prion protein. The prion protein, carried on the surface of nerve cells, whose normal job is still unknown. One sequence folds two ways, and the misfolded form stacks into fibres that template their own shape onto healthy copies.

α-Amylase. The enzyme in saliva and pancreatic juice that breaks starch down into sugars. It starts on the long chains before you have swallowed, cutting them along a trough that grips four sugars at a time.

Hexokinase. The enzyme that begins glycolysis, in every cell that burns glucose. It attaches a phosphate to the sugar, closing its two lobes around it so the ATP is not spent on a molecule of water instead.

Chymotrypsin. A digestive enzyme that cuts other proteins, which is why it is made switched off. The pancreas ships it as one inert chain and the intestine turns it on by cutting it, so the cell that built it is never digested by it.

Haemoglobin. The oxygen carrier in red blood cells: four chains, each holding one iron. Binding one oxygen changes the shape of the whole tetramer, so the next three bind more easily and all four are released together in tissue. Three of them here: the adult molecule, the sickle mutation, and the one a fetus makes.

Collagen. The structural protein of skin, bone and tendon, and about a third of the protein in your body. Three chains wind into a rope with a glycine at every third position, because nothing larger fits where the chains meet.

Ribonuclease A. Ribonuclease A, an enzyme from cow pancreas that cuts RNA. Anfinsen unfolded it and watched it fold back on its own, which is how we know a sequence carries the instructions for its own shape.

Insulin. The hormone that tells cells to take up glucose, made in the pancreas and cut out of a longer chain. Two short chains stapled by three disulfides, stored six at a time around a pair of zinc ions.

Myoglobin. The oxygen store of muscle: one chain wrapped around one iron. It was the first protein structure anyone ever solved, and it is still the clearest look at how a molecule is held in a binding site.
GFP. The green fluorescent protein, isolated from jellyfish. GFP is useful for tracking protein movements, gene expression, and cellular processes.

Ferritin. The iron store of the cell, a hollow shell built from 24 identical subunits. Loose iron is toxic and iron is essential, so ferritin oxidises it on the way in and keeps the mineral walled inside.

Rubisco. The enzyme that puts carbon into the biosphere: it sticks CO₂ from the air onto a five-carbon sugar. It is slow and it grabs O₂ by mistake, so plants make enormous amounts of it — there is more rubisco on Earth than any other protein.
Electronegativity. Some atoms pull shared electrons harder than others.
Covalent bond. Two atoms share a pair of electrons, and both count them as their own.
Polarity. Unequal sharing gives a molecule a positive end and a negative end.
Ionic bond. One atom takes the electron rather than sharing it. Opposite charges then hold the ions in a lattice.
Water molecule. Two hydrogens on one oxygen, held at 104.5°. The bend is why the pull toward oxygen does not cancel out.
Hydrogen bonding. A hydrogen bonded to oxygen or nitrogen carries a partial +, and it is pulled toward the partial − on the next O or N.
Cohesion & adhesion. Water sticks to itself, and to any surface it can hydrogen-bond to.
High specific heat. Heating water spends most of the energy breaking H-bonds, not raising the temperature.
Evaporative cooling. The fastest molecules escape first, and they take their energy with them.
Solvent properties. Water surrounds a charged particle and pulls it off its neighbours. Once every ion has a shell, the solid is gone.
The hydrophobic effect. Water pushes nonpolar molecules together to protect its own H-bond network.
Ice density anomaly. The frozen lattice holds molecules farther apart than the liquid does.
Ionization & pH. A few hundred million water molecules, and one has split into H⁺ and OH⁻. pH is the exponent on that count.
Transpiration. Water evaporating at the leaf pulls the column up behind it. Nothing pushes from the roots.
Temperature buffering. Cells and lakes change temperature slowly. Heat breaks H-bonds before it speeds molecules up.
Thermoregulation. Keeping body temperature steady while the outside moves. Sweat evaporates and takes the heat.
Endotherm. Heats itself from its own metabolism. Steady, and it costs most of what you eat.
Ectotherm. Takes its heat from outside. Cheap to run, and slow on a cold morning.
Osmosis. Water diffusing down its own gradient, from where there is more of it to where there is less.
Aquatic overwintering. Ice floats, so a lake freezes from the top and life persists below.
Buffers. A buffer trades protons back and forth, so pH barely moves.
Amphipathic. One end dissolves in water, the other cannot. Every membrane and micelle follows from that split.
DNA structure. Two antiparallel strands, paired base to base and twisted. Backbone outside, bases stacked in.
Dehydration synthesis. Monomers join by losing a water molecule. Every polymer bond is built this way.
Hydrolysis. Water is added back to break the bond. Digestion is this, run enzymatically.
Phospholipid. A charged head on two oily tails.
Phospholipid bilayer. Tails cannot face water, so they close into a double sheet with heads out. Water is what holds it together.
Functional group. A small cluster of atoms that behaves the same way whatever carbon skeleton it is bolted to.
Hydroxyl. OH. Makes the molecule polar, which is why sugars and alcohols dissolve.
Carbonyl. C=O. At the end of a chain it is an aldehyde, in the middle a ketone.
Carboxyl. COOH. Gives up its proton, so it is an acid. Every amino acid carries one.
Amino. NH₂. Takes a proton up, so it is a base. The other end of an amino acid.
Phosphate. PO₄. Negative, and where ATP holds the energy it is about to spend.
Methyl. CH₃. Nonpolar and unreactive, and a tag that switches genes quiet.
Polymer. Monomers joined into a chain by one bond, repeated. Three of the four classes are built this way.
Monosaccharide. One sugar unit. Same formula, different shape, and the shape is what an enzyme reads.
Polysaccharide. Sugars in a chain, for storage or for structure. Which one depends on how the link is turned.
Starch. Glucose linked α, which your enzymes can open. This is why bread is food.
Cellulose. The same glucose linked β. One flipped bond, and no enzyme you own will touch it.
Fatty acid. A long hydrocarbon tail with an acid group on the end. The tail is the energy.
Saturated. No double bonds, so the tails are straight and pack tight. Solid at room temperature.
Unsaturated. A double bond kinks the tail and stops it packing. Oils, and membrane fluidity.
Trans. A double bond with the kink straightened out by processing, so it packs like a saturated one.
Triglyceride. Three fatty acids on a glycerol. Not a polymer: no repeating unit, no chain.
Nucleotide. Phosphate, sugar, base. The phosphate is why the backbone is charged.
Adenine. A purine, two rings. Pairs with thymine in DNA and with uracil in RNA.
Thymine. A pyrimidine, one ring. DNA only, and two hydrogen bonds to adenine.
Guanine. A purine. Three hydrogen bonds to cytosine, which makes it the stronger pair.
Cytosine. A pyrimidine, and guanine’s partner in both DNA and RNA.
Uracil. Thymine without its methyl. RNA uses it; DNA does not, which helps repair spot damage.
Protein. Amino acids in a chain. The only class whose monomers come in twenty kinds.
Gene. A stretch of DNA that specifies one product. The order of its bases is the order of the amino acids.
Amino acid. Twenty kinds, and only the side chain differs between them.
R-group. The side chain: nonpolar, polar, acidic or basic. Those four categories decide how the chain folds.
Nonpolar. Greasy. Buried in the core away from water, and what holds the fold together.
Polar. Wet. Sits on the surface and hydrogen-bonds to water and to other side chains.
Acidic. Negative at cell pH. Aspartate and glutamate.
Basic. Positive at cell pH. Lysine, arginine, histidine.
Peptide bond. The covalent link between amino acids, and it survives cooking.
Primary structure. The sequence of amino acids, written by the gene.
Secondary structure. Helices and sheets, held by backbone H-bonds. The side chains play no part.
α-helix. The backbone coils, hydrogen-bonded four residues along. Keratin is almost all of it.
β-sheet. Strands lie alongside each other and bond across. Silk, and the barrel in GFP.
Turn. A short reversal so the chain can fold back on itself. Usually glycine or proline.
Tertiary structure. The overall 3D shape, driven entirely by the side chains.
Quaternary structure. Several folded chains docked into one unit. Hemoglobin’s four pass each other information one alone could not use.
R-group interactions. The side chains are what fold the protein: five forces, very different strengths.
Disulfide bridge. A covalent staple between two cysteines, roughly twenty times the other folding forces.
Van der Waals. Van der Waals forces are individually weak but act everywhere two surfaces touch, so they only add up where the fit is already close.
Protein folding. A linear chain of amino acids transforms into an ordered, three-dimensional structure that allows the protein to become biologically active.
Anfinsen’s experiment. Unfold ribonuclease completely, then take the denaturant away, and it folds back into working shape on its own. Nothing but the sequence directs it.
Denaturation. Heat or acid unfolds the shape while the peptide bonds hold. The sequence survives, everything built on it does not.
Protein function. A protein works by having one shape that fits one thing. Function is the fit.
Enzyme. Lowers a barrier and comes out unchanged.
Structural. Holds things up. Collagen, keratin, the cytoskeleton.
Transport. Carries or admits. Haemoglobin, channels, pumps.
Receptor. Binds a signal and changes shape, so a message crosses a membrane.
Motor. Turns ATP into movement. Myosin, kinesin, the flagellar motor.
Enzyme. A protein that lowers the barrier and comes out the other side unchanged.
Oxidoreductase. Moves electrons. The dehydrogenases that load NAD⁺ are these.
Transferase. Moves a group from one molecule to another. Hexokinase moves a phosphate.
Hydrolase. Breaks a bond using water. Amylase, and most of digestion.
Lyase. Breaks a bond without water, and often leaves a double bond behind.
Isomerase. Rearranges a molecule into its isomer, adding and removing nothing.
Ligase. Joins two molecules together, and spends ATP to do it.
Active site. A pocket in the tertiary structure where the substrate fits.
Specificity. One enzyme, one substrate, because the pocket has one shape.
Induced fit. Binding tightens the fit. The pocket is not rigid.
Activation energy. The hump a reaction has to get over before it can happen, however favourable the outcome.
Optimal conditions. Every enzyme has a pH and temperature where its shape holds, and a cliff past them.
Point mutation. One base changed, one amino acid swapped. Glu→Val on hemoglobin is enough to sickle a cell.
Silent. The codon changed and the amino acid did not. Most third-base changes are this.
Missense. One amino acid swapped for another. Sickle cell is a missense mutation.
Nonsense. A stop codon appears early and the chain is cut off where it stands.
Natural selection. Heritable variation plus unequal survival, repeated. Populations evolve; individuals never do.
Directional. One extreme is favoured and the whole population shifts that way.
Stabilising. The middle is favoured and both extremes are trimmed. Birth weight is the classic case.
Disruptive. Both extremes beat the middle, which is how one population can split in two.
Hydrophobic core. The tails meet in the middle, and that greasy layer is the whole barrier.
Selective permeability. Small and nonpolar crosses the greasy middle. Charged or large does not. Every transport mechanism is a way around that.
Fluid mosaic. Not a wall. A two-dimensional fluid, with the proteins free to drift sideways through it.
Membrane protein. Sits in the bilayer, greasy where it meets the tails. Almost everything the membrane does, a protein is doing.
Simple diffusion. Molecules spread because they move at random. At equilibrium the net flow stops, the motion does not.
Tonicity. Hypotonic, isotonic, hypertonic: a description of the solution outside, and a prediction about the cell.
Facilitated diffusion. A substance moves down its own gradient through a protein, which opens a path without pushing it.
Channel protein. A hole with a shape. Open it and the right ion falls through on its own.
Carrier protein. Binds its passenger, changes shape, lets go on the other side.
Active transport. A protein moves a substance against its gradient, spending ATP on every molecule it carries.
Electrochemical gradient. Pump something across and hold it there. The imbalance is now stored energy.
Endo- and exocytosis. Too big for any protein, so the membrane wraps around it and pinches off.
Cell theory. Every living thing is cells, and every cell comes from a cell.
Cell. The smallest thing that is alive. Nothing inside it is.
Surface area to volume. Double the width and volume grows eightfold while surface grows fourfold. The inside outruns its supply line.
Prokaryote. A cell with no nucleus and no internal compartments, small enough that it does not need them.
Eukaryote. A cell that keeps its DNA in a nucleus and divides its chemistry among membrane-bound compartments, which is what lets it be large.
Animal. No wall and no chloroplast. Its shape comes from the cytoskeleton alone.
Plant. Cellulose wall, chloroplasts, and one big vacuole holding the cell rigid.
Fungal. A wall like a plant’s but built from chitin, and no chloroplast.
Protist. Everything else with a nucleus. A dustbin category, and mostly single cells.
Cytoplasm. The crowded solution filling the cell, packed so densely with protein that a molecule can barely turn around.
Organelle. A room with its own chemistry, and its own membrane to keep it that way.
Nucleus. The DNA, kept apart from the machinery that reads it.
Ribosome. Reads mRNA and links amino acids into a protein. Bacteria and you inherited the same one from a shared ancestor.
Chloroplast. Two membranes and stacked discs, running the reaction that fills the atmosphere.
Cell wall. Outside the membrane, and rigid. A plant cell in fresh water swells until the wall pushes back, and that pressure is what holds the plant up.
Endosymbiotic theory. Mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria. They still carry their own DNA and their own ribosomes.
Redox. Oxidation is losing electrons, reduction is gaining them. Always both at once.
Glucose. A six-carbon sugar, and the cell’s default fuel. Its electrons are what respiration is after.
Pyruvate. Three carbons, and the fork in the road: with oxygen it goes on, without it does not.
Acetyl-CoA. Two carbons on a carrier, and the doorway into the cycle.
ATP. The cell spends this, not glucose. A rechargeable battery, recharged about your body weight a day.
Oxygen. Oxygen never touches the glucose; it waits at the end of the electron transport chain and accepts the spent electrons.
Electron carriers. NAD⁺ and FAD collect the electrons stripped off glucose and hand them to the chain. The pool is small, so it has to be given back.
Proton gradient. The chain pumps H⁺ to one side. The imbalance itself is stored energy, and it is what the cell actually banks.
Chemiosmosis. Protons fall back through a turbine, and the turbine makes ATP. Mitochondria run this, chloroplasts run this, and so does every bacterium.
Mitchell’s hypothesis. Mitchell proposed a proton gradient in place of the chemical intermediate everyone was hunting. Chloroplasts then made ATP in the dark when an acid bath supplied the gradient.
Substrate-level phosphorylation. An enzyme hands a phosphate straight to ADP. Direct, and a small fraction of the total.
Oxidative phosphorylation. ATP made from the gradient instead of by hand. This is where almost all of it comes from.
Mitochondrion. Two membranes, and the inner one is folded because the chain lives in it. Area is the point.
Cellular respiration. Glucose is taken apart one pair of electrons at a time, and the energy is banked as ATP.
Glycolysis. Glucose splits into two pyruvate in the cytosol. Two ATP spent, four made, two carriers loaded.
Pyruvate oxidation. One carbon leaves as CO₂ and the rest becomes acetyl-CoA. The first carbon you breathe out.
Krebs cycle. Two more carbons leave as CO₂, and every turn loads three NADH, one FADH₂, one ATP. The eight intermediates are the conveyor that does it.
Electron transport chain. Electrons fall from carrier to carrier, and every drop pumps protons across the membrane.
Fermentation. No oxygen, so the chain stops and the carriers stay full. Fermentation empties them so glycolysis can keep going.
Lactate. A dead end. Pyruvate takes its own electrons back, and your muscles feel it.
Ethanol. Two carbons; the third leaves as CO₂. Yeast’s exit, and it is bread and beer.
Base pairing. A with T, G with C, held by hydrogen bonds. Either strand is enough to rebuild the other.
Antiparallel. The two strands run in opposite directions, and every copying machine can only work one way along a strand.
Chromosome. One very long DNA molecule wound onto protein spools, so two metres of it fits in a nucleus.
DNA replication. The strands separate and each one templates a new partner. One molecule becomes two.
Helicase. Unwinds the double helix and holds the two strands apart.
DNA polymerase. Adds bases to the new strand, and checks the last one it added.
Primase. Lays a short RNA start, because polymerase cannot begin from nothing.
Ligase. Seals the nicks between the lagging strand’s backward pieces.
Topoisomerase. Cuts and rejoins ahead of the fork so the helix does not knot.
Semiconservative. Every new molecule keeps one old strand. The original is never discarded, only shared out.
Proofreading. The copying enzyme checks its last base and backs up to fix it. Errors survive at about one in a billion.
Leading and lagging. One new strand runs continuously, the other in backward pieces. The asymmetry is forced by the antiparallel strands.
Transcription. One gene is copied into RNA. The DNA itself never leaves the nucleus, which is the whole reason for a messenger.
RNA. One strand, ribose, uracil for thymine. It carries messages, and it also builds things and catalyses.
mRNA. A working copy of one gene, sent out to the ribosome so the original stays put.
RNA processing. Introns cut out, exons joined. Splice the same transcript differently and one gene yields several proteins.
Translation. The ribosome reads the message three bases at a time and builds the chain the message names.
The genetic code. The rule that assigns each codon to one amino acid. It is nearly identical in every organism alive, which is why the code is evidence of common ancestry.
Codon. Three bases in mRNA that specify one amino acid. Sixty-four codons cover twenty amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one.
Start. AUG. Marks where translation begins, and sets the frame for everything after it.
Stop. UAA, UAG, UGA. No amino acid at all. The ribosome lets go.
Sense. The other sixty. Each names one amino acid, and most amino acids answer to several.
tRNA. An adaptor: one end pairs with the codon, the other carries the matching amino acid.
Reading frame. Where the reading starts. Shift it by one base and every codon after that is different.
Mutation. Any change to the sequence. Most do nothing, some are harmful, and a few are the raw material of evolution.
Mutagen. Something from outside that damages the sequence. The other way a mutation happens, besides miscopying.
Ultraviolet. Fuses two neighbouring thymines into a kink the copying enzyme reads wrong.
Chemical. Benzene, aflatoxin, tobacco tar. Some mimic a base, some jam themselves between them.
Ionising radiation. X-rays and gamma rays cut the backbone outright, sometimes both strands at once.
Frameshift. Insert or delete one base and the frame shifts. Everything downstream is nonsense.
Gene expression. Which genes a cell is currently reading. Every cell holds the same genome and runs a different part of it.
Transcription factor. A protein that binds near a gene and changes how often it is read. A dial, not a switch.
Activator. Binds and makes the gene easier to read, so more of the protein gets made.
Repressor. Binds and gets in the way, so the gene is read less. Rarely off, just quieter.
Differentiation. A neuron and a liver cell hold identical DNA. They differ in which of it is switched on.
The central dogma. DNA is copied to RNA and RNA is read into protein. Information travels one way along that chain.
Meselson–Stahl. Three hypotheses, one experiment with heavy nitrogen, and only semiconservative survived the first round.
Hershey–Chase. Label the phage protein and the phage DNA separately, and only the DNA goes into the cell.
Avery–MacLeod–McCarty. Destroy the protein in a cell extract and it still transforms bacteria. Destroy the DNA and it stops.
Photograph 51. An X-ray pattern showing a helix of constant diameter with the phosphate backbone outside. It set the dimensions any model had to fit.
Light energy. Photons arrive in fixed sizes. A pigment either absorbs one whole or does not absorb it.
Pigment. A molecule that absorbs some wavelengths and reflects the rest. You see the wavelengths it threw away.
Carotenoid. Orange and yellow. Catches what chlorophyll misses, and is there all summer, masked.
Anthocyanin. Red and purple, and mostly made fresh rather than unmasked. Also most red flowers and fruit.
Phycobilin. Red algae and cyanobacteria. Catches the blue-green that is all that reaches any depth.
Retinal. The one in your own eye. A pigment absorbing light is not a plant idea.
Chlorophyll. Absorbs red and blue hard, green barely at all. Plants are green because green is the light they waste.
Photosystem. A few hundred pigments funnelling energy to one pair of chlorophylls that lets an electron go.
Photosystem II. First in the chain despite the name. It splits water and starts the electrons moving.
Photosystem I. Second. Another photon re-energises the electrons, and NADPH gets loaded.
Photolysis. Water is split to replace the electron the photosystem lost. The oxygen is what is left over.
Thylakoid. A flattened sac inside the chloroplast. It is a sealed compartment, which is the only reason a gradient can build.
Light reactions. Light drives electrons down a chain, protons pile up in the sac, and the turbine makes ATP. The same chain as respiration, run the other way: light pushes the electrons uphill.
NADPH. The reduced carrier the light reactions load. Same job as NADH, spent building sugar instead of making ATP.
Calvin cycle. Spends the ATP and NADPH to build sugar from CO₂. It runs in daylight; it just does not need photons directly.
Van Helmont’s willow. A willow gained seventy-five kilograms in five years while its soil lost almost none. He concluded water; the missing source was the air.
Carbon fixation. Rubisco attaches CO₂ from the air onto a sugar, and that carbon is now plant. A tree is mostly rebuilt atmosphere.
C3. Rubisco fixes carbon straight into the Calvin cycle. Most plants, and it struggles in heat.
C4. Carbon is caught in one cell and handed to another, so rubisco never meets much oxygen.
CAM. Pores open at night and the carbon is held until morning. Cacti, in deserts.
Stomata. Pores in the leaf. Open for CO₂ and water escapes; shut to keep water and the carbon supply stops.
Photorespiration. Rubisco binds O₂ instead of CO₂, and the plant spends ATP undoing the result. Worse when it is hot and the pores are shut.
Photosynthesis. Light energy into chemical bonds, using water and air. Respiration read backwards, and the source of both.
Structure ↔ Function. Show me everything where a shape is the explanation.
Energy Flow. Show me everything where the question is where the energy went.
Information Flow. Show me everything where the meaning is in the encoding and not in the chemistry.
